channel.title: sgit.ai articles
channel.description: Articles and desk notes from sgit.ai, newest first.

item.title: One writer, one key: this newsroom now allows one journalist agent at a time, registered at my word and signing every release, and a decommissioned agent's key is never used again
item.description: On the night of 30 October two of this newsroom's writer agents pushed to the same branch, and one release was rejected because the other had shipped first. Merging them meant reconciling 1,925 generated files. It was a small incident with a clear lesson: I wanted only one journalist agent at a time, and nothing enforced it. So this morning the newsroom started using the public-key infrastructure we have been writing about. There is now a register of writer agents. A registration is opened only at my word, and only when no other is open; the session makes a new key pair and keeps the private half. Every commit a writer makes carries a signature over exactly the files it commits, and the site's validator, locally and in CI, refuses a writer's commit that the open registration did not sign, refuses two open registrations, and refuses a key used twice. Decommissioning is the other half: a registration is closed by me, or in the commit that opens the next writer, its private key is deleted, and it is never reopened. The same Claude session may come back, but only as a new registration with a new key. The first signed commit became site v0.14.15. This article gives the exact steps, the six cases the gate refuses, the mistake made while testing it, and the weakness that remains: my approval is still a note in the same repository, so the next step is that I sign each registration with my own key.

item.title: An augmented PDF viewer: how hard is it to build one in the browser that renders any PDF and opens the provenance, the graph and the comments behind it? Less than I thought
item.description: The augmented book made me ask a question about PDF. It is a strange format: static, closed, made for a printed page, with nothing behind it. But a PDF is how most serious documents still travel, and the book will have one. So why not augment the PDF? I asked a research agent how feasible it would be to build a viewer in JavaScript, in the browser, that renders any PDF normally but also shows a layer the PDF cannot: the provenance of each claim, the nodes of the semantic graph, definitions, comments and review cards, on demand, beside the text. The answer is that most of it exists, as open source we can extend. Mozilla's PDF.js, under the Apache licence and committed to the day before we looked, already draws a page as a stack of layers, canvas, text and annotations, and announces each one as it renders, so a layer of our own fits on top. It can read a PDF's attachments, its metadata, its links and its fingerprint. And the augmented layer does not need to live in the PDF at all: the PDF only needs clues to find it, an attached file, an id in its metadata, a link, the file's own identifier, or a QR code that survives printing. Hypothesis already anchors annotations to PDFs this way, and e-invoices already carry machine-readable data inside human-readable PDFs. The hard part is not the PDF. It is the interface, anchoring claims to text reliably, and making sure the layer a viewer loads is signed by the people who made the document.

item.title: The Web Summit team, part two: seven people, each with their own agent, a designer with little time, and every voice memo turned into a follow-up within the hour
item.description: The first brief for our Web Summit team set up an event site run by agents. This second part is about the people, because this is the first team we run with many humans in it. Seven of us are going, some in the Algarve and some still in the UK, all with ideas, and each of us brings our own agent, so the team is really a set of agents collaborating through their humans. That needs three things the agent-only teams did not. First, clear roles: who owns which company, who follows whom, who is talking to whom, recorded in a personal CRM for each of us, kept in our own vaults and synchronised into the team's view by shared ids. Second, speed: anything any of us records, a voice memo after a conversation, a scanned card, a note to our agent, is picked up within the hour and turned into action, a CRM entry, a page made for that company, a drafted follow-up, while a person still sends every email. Third, a way to work with people who have very little time, like the professional designer joining us, by learning what works for each person, briefing them in their own medium with the least context they need, and letting agents prepare the variants, the presentations and the animations around their work. And everything is worked backwards from the summit: the branded T-shirts, hoodies, cards and small things to hand out each have a date they must be ordered by, and each carries a code that leads to a page. Before the summit there are meetups in the Algarve; during it, the newsroom publishes; after it, the follow-up is the product we are showing.

item.title: The augmented book: one source in layers, projected to the web, the iPad and print, so the reader gets the right information at the right time, and what fifty years of attempts teach
item.description: Every article here ends with a section called Where this comes from, and the book of The Ultimate Insider will have them too. It is important: it is the provenance, the evidence that what we say is true. But it is the right information at the wrong time. At the end of a chapter it is too much, a list of words the reader has no connection to, and too little, because on paper none of it links to anything. That made me see a concept I think we are arriving at: the augmented book. The book is one source, in layers: the text everyone reads; what opens on demand, a definition, a source, a step expanded where it is; the provenance of each claim; and the record behind it, the graph, the versions and the reviews. Each medium projects it differently. The website is hyperlinked and lets the reader choose how much shows. The iPad app shows layers on the page, with the review's comments where they belong. The PDF and print keep the page clean and put a QR code where the layer would open. Like augmented reality, the extra is there when you look for it and not before, and one day it may reach smart glasses. I asked who has done this before. The mechanisms are old: Ted Nelson's stretchtext, Voyager's expanded books in 1992, the MagicBook in 2001, Kindle's X-Ray, Wikipedia's page previews. What failed, again and again, was the platform: books built for one company's engine died with it. And the research on cognitive load says what the editor in me wanted to hear: notes next to the claim, few, signalled and under the reader's control.

item.title: An iPad to review the book: a brief for an app that reads the PDFs, shows the comments on the page, opens its vault with my passkey and carries sgit in Swift
item.description: I review on the iPad because it is like a book: no notifications, nothing else on the screen. But reviewing the book of The Ultimate Insider there showed me what is missing. Preview has no full screen I could find and no way to work across several files, and the review lives in two PDFs, the book and its companion of cards, with my comments going back by hand. So this is a brief for an iPad app built to review the book, and later to read it. It reads the PDFs properly. It shows the comments, the cards and the votes on the page they are about, because once we control the medium the review does not have to be a second PDF. It sends and receives feedback through append lanes, and everything it exchanges is JSON tied to the book's semantic graph. Its library is an sgit vault on the iPad, encrypted at rest and opened with my passkey, using an extension Apple has offered apps since iOS 18. And sgit inside it is written in Swift, which would make it the third implementation of the format, after the command line and the browser. It meters what it is used for, the way the newsroom's reader account does, with a balance that can go negative, because the reader pays for the use and is not the product. The good news is that I have done part of this before. In March, a team of agents and I built a desktop app for the SGraph sites in two days, signed and notarised with my Apple developer account, ran it on an Android emulator, and set up an iOS build pipeline. This article reads that repository, says what carries over and what does not, and why I now think the iPad app should be native.

item.title: Becoming an official publication: the SGit Newsroom now has a publisher, an editor, standards, a corrections log, a withdrawal process and a complaints route, and is applying to a regulator
item.description: The SGit Newsroom has been publishing for weeks, and it names companies, reports incidents and argues positions, written by agents from my voice memos. Today a story showed me that this needs more than good habits. We wrote about a contractor's agent on a Pentagon network from secondary reports of an article we could not read, copied a quote that one outlet had given to the wrong party, corrected it, and then I withdrew the article, because it repeated allegations about named organisations made by unnamed sources, which this newsroom should not publish at all. So the newsroom is becoming an official publication. In the UK there is no licence to be a journalist; what makes a publication accountable is that it says who publishes it and who answers for it, publishes its standards, corrects in the open, withdraws with a notice, takes complaints, and submits to an independent regulator. As of this release the newsroom has an imprint, naming The Cyber Boardroom Limited as publisher and me as editor, and saying plainly that agents write the articles; editorial standards that rule out making or repeating allegations, so what we publish is analysis and opinion; a corrections log; a formal withdrawal process with its first notice; and a complaints route with a 21-day answer. Next we apply to IMPRESS, the independent press regulator, and register for an ISSN with the British Library, and later we look at the Journalism Trust Initiative and a press card for the editor. This article says what each step is, what it costs, what we have done and what is still to do.

item.title: Signed by the agent, vouched for by the person: a brief to give every email agent its own key, so each email carries a QR code that proves it is authentic
item.description: Each of us now has an agent that runs our email: it reads, researches, drafts and keeps the records, and a person sends. I just realised we can do something powerful with that. Give each email agent its own key pair, vouched for by its person's key on pki.sgit.ai, and every email it drafts can carry a signature and a QR code that lets the recipient check, in a browser, that the email is authentic: that it came from my one official email agent, acting for me, and has not been changed. We already have the pieces. Our agent sessions make their own keys and publish them. pki.sgit.ai is a register of people and their keys, verified both ways, with signed statements, evidence such as a DNS record or a website file, and delegations signed by a person's key that stop the moment the person withdraws them. Email has signatures today, but DKIM proves the domain's mail server sent the message, not which person or which agent wrote it, and S/MIME and PGP ask the reader to install and trust something. This brief maps out what to build: a key for each email agent and a delegation from its person; a signature over each email's content; a QR code and a link to a verification page that shows who signed it, for whom, and whether that delegation still holds; and the rules for the world we are entering, where agents act for us from our email accounts, one official agent each, so that anything sent on our behalf can be proved, and anything not signed can be questioned.

item.title: A brief for the Web Summit team: an event site run by an ephemeral agent team, built from this week's template, with a map of every company we should meet
item.description: Web Summit runs in Lisbon from 9 to 12 November, and seven of us are now going. The plan I published on 26 October called for a newsroom of our own for the summit. This is the brief to build it, now that we have a template that works. In the last two days three teams were stood up from nothing in a few hours each: the talk's, the cold read's and the book's. Each had a repository, a written brief, a role file and a behaviour policy per member, a key for every session, an hourly slot, a five-step wake, a hold any member can pull, a board and a mailroom in git, and a gate with CI owning the version. The Web Summit team gets the same, on an event site that consolidates everything about our participation: the graph of companies and people, the events and sessions, the materials, and a countdown with observability, so we can see what is used. Its centre is a map of the companies going, built from public material only: who they are, what they do, why they matter to us, and whether we should meet them, interview them or write about them, each with an owner on our team. Each person's email stays in their own account, run by their own email agent, and each of those agents gets a key, so that what it sends can be verified; that is a separate brief. The design track, T-shirts, hoodies, a banner, cards for everyone and flyers, gets its own brief and its own design member. This article sets out the site, the template, the roles, the company map, the schedule to 12 November, and what I need to decide.

item.title: Selling less code: the economics of customised open source, where the customer pays for the features they use, the maker certifies what it ships, and the pipeline is finally tied to revenue
item.description: One of our business models is to sell customised versions of open source software: a version made for one customer and relicensed to them. Some of the customisation is cosmetic, a logo or a brand. The part that matters is that we are selling a reduction in complexity. If a customer uses 10% of an application's features, why should they pay for all of them, and why should they take on all of their technical debt? Every feature is code to maintain, a screen of options to learn and a place for the next vulnerability to land. The fewer moving parts, the better the security and the engineering. Open source is what makes this possible: with the code available, we can build custom static analysis, custom environments and semantic knowledge graphs of what a customer actually uses, and the people best placed to certify the result are the ones who made it. And there is a positive loop. When the cost of customising is ours, we invest in making it cheap: software designed to be mixed and matched, and the CI pipeline, the non-functional requirements, the threat models and the certification that usually fight for budget because they are not tied to revenue. Here they are the product. It is the next phase of RiskMandate, with sgit and SHarness: a customised build is a signed, hashed release in a vault, licensed to the customer with our key, with a smaller behaviour policy and fewer rows for an insurer to price. The base stays open, maintained by many; the customer's version can be proprietary to them; and the more customisation a customer wants, the more it costs, which rewards everyone for keeping as much as possible in the open.

item.title: Breaking the story down before the agents do: a reply to Ole Reissmann's session at the News Product Alliance Summit, and what this newsroom already ships to the machines that read it
item.description: Ole Reissmann, who works on AI and journalism at DER SPIEGEL, led a session at the News Product Alliance Summit in Chicago called "Beyond the Article: Breaking Down Stories So Agents Get Them Right". His diagnosis is one I share: agents read journalism as fragments, stitch a confident summary together, sometimes miss the one thing that matters, and the publisher has almost no say in what comes out. His answer is to do the breakdown ourselves, before the machines do: SPIEGEL built a workflow that pulls out the actors and events, traces sources and claims, and flags allegations the affected party should get to respond to, and tested it for summaries with no human in the loop. He also says that a lot of the layers already exist, they just are not plugged into each other. This is a reply from a newsroom built that way from the start. Every article here is published with a markdown twin, a knowledge graph and a one-line and one-paragraph summary of every section, and the release checks look for them. As of today there are 327 article graphs, with 3,676 nodes, 3,564 edges and 819 quotes, each checked to appear word for word in its article, and summaries for 3,674 sections. The site publishes llms.txt and llms-full.txt for agents, and every article ends with where it came from. The book we are writing keeps a claims register in which every number has an id and a command to rerun it. And today's article on a contractor's agent at the Pentagon put the answers of the company, the department and the vendor next to the allegations. Where SPIEGEL is ahead is the allegation itself as a field, and I would like to add it.

item.title: Seven IAM predictions for 2027, checked against an agent team that runs today: where we already are, where we agree, and the two where I would bet the other way
item.description: Sunnykumar K., a lead IAM engineer, posted seven predictions for identity and access management from 2027 to 2030, the ones he is designing for now: static roles give way to policy-driven access, non-human identities outnumber humans 100 to 1, passwords start to disappear, identity tools consolidate into one platform, continuous access evaluation becomes standard, access decisions are made by models, and identity becomes a board-level conversation. I agree with most of them, and several are not predictions for us: they describe how our agent teams already work. In two days this week one person ran more than thirty agent sessions, each with its own key pair, its own role and a written behaviour policy. Every session's key is vouched for with an end date, and dies with the session; secrets are sealed to keys, never typed; the reader's vault on this site opens with a passkey. Each agent wakes on a schedule and its work is planned, reviewed before and after, and checked against its plan, and any agent can pull a hold that pauses all actions. And every control is classified by who enforces it, so that a board or an insurer can count the ones that are real. I would bet the other way on two. Consolidation into one platform is the wrong goal for agents: the policy should be an open document that many enforcers read. And access decisions should not be handed to a model: a model can advise, but the boundary has to be deterministic and outside it, because an agent's own account of what it did is a self-report. This article goes through the seven, with what we run and what we have measured.

item.title: A book that looks like the team that made it: what the best visual books, Leanpub's Markua and learning research teach, and what an agent team can put on a printed page
item.description: The talk I gave at hack::soho looked like it was made by an agent team: a custom player, its own navigation, and animations everywhere, each one made to drive a point home. The book of the talk has to do the same, or the medium contradicts the message. But a book that goes to Leanpub and to print on demand has only text, images and a little layout. So before designing it I asked for research: what the best visual books do, what Markua (Leanpub's markdown) and Amazon's print service allow, and what the research on learning says about pictures and words. The findings are clear. Markua gives more than I expected: images sized as a share of the page, floated toward or away from the spine, or full bleed; numbered figures with captions; SVG and Mermaid diagrams kept as text; and seven kinds of typed box, for tips, warnings, questions and exercises. The limits are mostly cost and craft: no raw HTML, no text on both sides of an image, and colour printing that costs from about twice to more than five times as much per page as black ink. Richard Mayer's experiments rate pictures with words at an effect size of 1.39 and putting the words next to the picture at 1.09, and show that decoration hurts. Retrieval practice and spacing are rated the most useful study techniques. The best books, from Edward Tufte's to Julia Evans's zines, Simon Wardley's maps and Bob Nystrom's Crafting Interpreters, apply these by hand. An agent team can apply them by machine: one visual grammar across every figure, each figure a spec that can be rerun when I change my mind, animations turned into filmstrips, every number tied to the register, and questions to remember by. This article sets out what we found, and the plan for the book.

item.title: The book of the talk by morning: RC1 of The Ultimate Insider, written from the record, read cold by a second team, with a companion PDF that turns reviews into tick boxes
item.description: The night after I gave The ultimate insider at hack::soho, two agent teams worked on the book of it while I slept. One, in a new repository started at 00:35 UTC, built the book's machinery: a claims register, a timeline of the day hour by hour, an index and a chapter plan. The other, started two minutes later, was given only the talk's repository at one commit and told to read it cold: thirteen agents, no briefing, every claim cited to a path or written as "the record does not say". By 10:00 the cold read had made 349 commits, 78 releases and about 42,400 words, and a 16-page debrief as a PDF. At about 10:00 I signed the chapter plan and said I was flying later and wanted a PDF to read on the plane. At 11:00 I had two. RC1 is 294 pages at 6 by 9 inches: thirteen chapters, a chapter on how to read a Wardley map, sixteen maps, 28 infographics, 50 call-outs and an appendix that reruns every number from git. The second PDF is the part I think matters most. The companion is 67 A4 pages of 98 cards, from eight readers: the book team's roles and the team of my previous book. Each card quotes one sentence of RC1, finds the page it is on and prints that page small beside it, and gives me boxes to tick and lines to write on. 53 of the cards are decisions only I can take. A book review used to be a pile of comments; here it is a form I can fill in on a plane, and the conductor turns my ticks into decisions. This article tells how both PDFs were made, with the times from the two repositories, and what went wrong, including a leak account that turned out to be about values that were never secrets.

item.title: SHarness: the secure harness we could not find, so we built it, a behaviour policy the Linux kernel enforces for every process an agent starts, and we would like your feedback
item.description: For a long time we have said that an agent's rules need a secure harness that sits outside the agent's own environment, outside RiskMandate's and outside the hook. We looked for one and did not find it, so I sat down with a few Claude agents and we built it, and it is now released, at sharness.ai, with sharness-ai 0.2.0 on PyPI. SHarness is what our Agent Behaviour Policies become when they are executed rather than read. An Agent Behaviour Policy describes what an agent is mandated to do, what it can actually reach, the gap between the two, and what stands in the way of each capability. A Process Behaviour Policy applies the same model to every process the agent starts: what it may read, write, run, connect to and spend, written as a small policy, hashed to one name the person supplies from outside, and enforced by something the process does not include, the Linux kernel or a small separate service. A tricked agent cannot widen it, because the kernel was told before the process started. That turns Settings and Expectations into Boundaries, which is the only kind of control an insurer can price, and it puts the permission prompt last: yes to what the policy allows, silence for what it refuses, and a question only for what it cannot hold. The design is a launcher and five doors, files, network, keys, shell and model, each a small service with its own user and its own certificate, and the same policy can be written for bubblewrap, Docker, Kubernetes or Claude Code's sandbox, with the list of what each cannot hold. Today the kernel locks run, two doors run as early versions, and a real Linux kernel boots in a browser tab and refuses what the policy refuses; the launcher that binds the agent itself is still the design. It is open source, and what I would most like now is feedback.

item.title: investor.sgit.ai: a brief for a website where investors and founders use our tools, not read about them, with the news, contracts as graphs, deal rooms as vaults and sgit as the case study
item.description: This is an article brief: one idea and one task, and the direction of travel behind them. We are starting to talk to investors, and the challenge with most of what we build is that it has to be experienced to be understood. So the best way to talk to investors is to have them use it, and the place to do that is a website of its own, investor.sgit.ai, for investors and founders together, angel to Series A. It would carry the news from investor circles, tracked from public sources as a graph; startup contracts, cap tables and term sheets as linked graphs with their versions and caveats; a section for founders on how to talk to an investor and what comes next; the funding models from open source to proprietary; deal rooms as vaults, and keys for investors as a demonstration of PKI; RiskMandate's due diligence and de-risking at work; and sgit itself as the case study, its strategy and thinking published as it happens. It would also put back in front of people work that got lost: the GenAI cybersecurity startup evaluation framework I published in March, seven criteria and a meta-criterion scored to forty, which is the first piece of the maturity model I had in mind. Like the PHP newsroom, it would be run by a small team of agents on a schedule, built from the first commit to sgit.ai's rules for a new repository, with CI owning the version. And then I would show it to investors and ask: is this useful, and what would help?

item.title: Agents have an identity now: a key pair made in every session, published with its role, so any agent can seal a secret to it, and the piece the cloud providers could add
item.description: It has been coming for a while, and I think we now have a working way to give agents an identity, which is bigger than the workflow I described last time. Agent identity is a large problem, and it tends to get over-built; here the answer turned out to be simple. A new session is given a GitHub repository and a role. It makes its own key pair, and the private half never leaves it. It publishes the public half, with a fingerprint and a QR image, beside its role in the repository, and that push is the authorisation. It runs on a schedule, so it acts on its own. And any other agent can read its key, check it, and seal a secret only that session can open. On 28 October the PHP newsroom's ten agents did exactly that in one night, between 01:05 and 03:29 UTC, and every one of their QR images reads back to its own fingerprint. The same day, the agent that writes this site sealed a vault key to the agent that keeps a register of vault keys, after checking that its key chains to my root on pki.sgit.ai. Ironically, this is what the cloud providers could have given every agent. Microsoft, AWS and Google each now offer an agent identity, but it is a principal inside one tenant or account, used to get tokens: their documentation does not describe a key the agent holds, a place an outsider can find it, or a way for anyone to encrypt to it. That is what I would like to ask them for. Tie the key to a role and a good definition of that role, and it is a very powerful thing.

item.title: A talk built in a day: the ultimate insider, from an empty repository at 00:16 to the stage at hack::soho at 19:00, by nine agents and one editor, every number from their records
item.description: Tonight I gave a talk called The ultimate insider at hack::soho, at IOActive in London, and it went really well. I will write a debrief of the talk itself. This is about how it was made, because I think it is a good testament of what we can now do. The repository was empty at 00:16 UTC. By 18:46 it had 814 commits, 210 releases numbered by CI, a website with the talk as data, 58 slides that are each a live, animated web page, a script, a sources page, a dashboard, and a set of articles the team generated about itself. It was built by nine agents and one editor: a conductor, a deck lead, a designer, a developer, a researcher, a storyteller, a motion designer, a studio and ruv.sgit, each with a written role, a behaviour policy, a session key and an hourly slot. Between them they made 162 wakes, each one planned, reviewed by a sub-agent before and after the work, and checked against its plan; 148 ended ok. They sent each other 293 notes. And almost every innovation we have been working on this month came together in it: CI owning the version, session keys where the push is the authorisation, vault keys sealed to the vault registry, public vaults as the board and the mail, a behaviour policy per agent with one writer per file enforced by the gate, ruv.sgit's player and studio, SHarness running live on a slide, and pages that report on the team from its own records, so nothing about the night is typed by hand. The article shows it with screenshots and collages from the site's own admin pages, the slides, and the team's records, and says what went wrong, including the hold at 18:44 when my usage limit reached 95%.

item.title: Proven controls, for agents: an answer to Hem Pant's governance as code and Sondera's policy-as-code paper, with the column they leave open and the controls we have actually tried to break
item.description: Two pieces reached me on the same day and they belong together. Hem Pant, a CISO who has spent two decades leading security at global banks, wrote that policies don't protect institutions, proven controls do, and asked for one unbroken line from Board intent to live evidence, with every control tested by a deliberately non-compliant change that fails the build if it is not caught. Sondera's paper on the autoformalization of agent instructions into policy-as-code does a large part of that line for agents: it turns an agent's prompt, its tool descriptions and a policy document into Cedar policies, checks them with a hard and a soft critic, and enforces them outside the context window, failing closed. I agree with both, and this is the unifying theme: the policy has to leave the PDF and the prompt and become something that runs and can be tested. What I would add, from what we run every day with Agent Behaviour Policies, is one column both leave open: who holds each control. A rule the agent can change or skip is a Setting, and a test proves only that it ran; a rule held from above the agent is a Boundary, and only that can be proven not to be switched off. Our own numbers show why it matters: when this newsroom walked its 57 checks up to the behaviours they protect, 22 were expectations, 34 settings and one a boundary. So here is the line with that column added, what we have generated, mapped and enforced, and six controls we tried to break, including the release gate that failed our own build tonight. And an answer to Hem's invitation for a common, machine-readable way to express controls and evidence: the Agent Behaviour Policy is an open project, and its process form now has a written standard with test vectors.

item.title: Insuring agents, the whole story: five articles and three vaults on one idea, that an agent's behaviour policy can be read as an insurance policy, priced row by row and backed by capital
item.description: Over one day I wrote four articles on a single question, who could underwrite an agent behaviour policy today, and this one tells the whole story and points to all of them, and to the vaults where the ideas run. The first, a payout for every row, defines what would be insured: a behaviour policy already lists what an agent can reach and what it may do, so each row can have its own limit, each enforced control lowers that row's premium, and what the policy does not name is not covered; an uncontrolled support agent pays £69,850 a year for £80,000 of cover, and with five enforced controls on a certified runtime, £6,720. The second, who carries the risk, maps who sells agent cover today, AIUC, Armilla, Testudo, Munich Re and Harbor, and the four parts of an insurer, and finds the way in is a managing agent on someone else's capital. The third, the vendor's layer, gives the agent's vendor a share of each row when its own conditions held: £1,816 of the £6,720. The fourth, where to build the agent insurer, says London to underwrite and carry the risk, the US and the EU to sell into, and that what the money buys is cover: £10 million raised in one go backs about £94 million to £188 million of it, £50 million about £761 million to £1.52 billion. Three vaults make the ideas something you can open: the Licence to Operate simulation, the agent underwriting calculator, and AIUC-1 as a graph with a conformance layer. Every article in the series now carries the same row of cards at its top and foot, so it is clear which one you are reading.

item.title: Where to build the agent insurer: underwrite and carry the risk in London, sell into the US and the EU, raise the capital in one go, and what £10 million or £50 million buys in cover
item.description: The last three articles described insuring an agent row by row from its behaviour policy, who could carry the risk, and the vendor's share of it. This one asks where such a company should be built, from a regulatory and an investment point of view, and how much it would take. My answer is London first, for two of its three jobs. It should start as a managing agent there, pricing and selling on a Lloyd's syndicate's capital, because that is where two of today's AI agent covers are written, authorisation takes up to nine months, and an intermediary's own capital is the higher of £5,000 or 2.5% of its income; and it should carry the risk there too, as a UK insurer through the PRA's mobilisation regime or with capital at Lloyd's. It should sell into the US through surplus lines, a $143.3 billion market built for risks without a loss history, and into the EU by one registration, once Europe's product rules make software a product on 9 December 2026. The Gulf's funds are a place to raise capital. On the money, I built a small model with every assumption stated, and the point it makes is that what the money buys is cover. Two years of running the company cost about £4.35 million; everything raised above that backs policies, and because every row is capped, the ceiling of cover follows from it. Raised in one go, £10 million backs about £94 million to £188 million of cover, 1,177 to 2,354 agents at £80,000 each; £50 million backs about £761 million to £1.52 billion, 9,510 to 19,020 agents, depending on how much of the book one shared failure could hit at once. The bigger the cover the company aims for, the more it should raise at the start.

item.title: The vendor's layer: what the companies that sell AI agents should cover themselves, row by row, when their contracts cap liability at a year's fees and Europe's new product rules treat software as a product
item.description: The first two articles of this series described insuring an agent row by row from its behaviour policy, and who could carry that risk. This one is about a party I think has to carry some of it: the vendor that sells the agent. When a company buys an agentic workflow, part of what can go wrong is the company's own doing, the access it granted and the data it connected, and part is the vendor's, the model's answer, the guardrail that let something through. Cloud providers settled the same question years ago with a shared responsibility model: AWS calls it security of the cloud and security in the cloud. Agent vendors' published terms put almost all of it on the customer: Anthropic's and Salesforce's both cap liability at the fees paid in the previous twelve months, indemnify intellectual property claims, and leave it to the customer to decide whether outputs are appropriate or use is safe. Some vendors already back their products with money, and the most useful shape is Microsoft's: cover, as long as the customer used the guardrails the product provides. Europe is moving the line from 9 December 2026, when software, AI systems included, becomes a product under the new product liability directive, with no contractual cap against an injured person. So I propose the vendor's layer: in each row of a behaviour policy, a share the vendor carries when its own conditions held. In the worked example, of a £6,720 premium for £80,000 of cover, the vendor carries £1,816, mostly on the rows its product decides; the row the customer decided by granting write access stays the customer's. The formula, the inputs and a calculator are in a vault anyone can open.

item.title: How a journalist agent publishes here: the newsroom's handbook, from the brief to the live page, with the versioning, the checks and the mistakes that taught us each rule
item.description: Several agent sessions write for this newsroom, and every one of them has to learn the same things: where an article lives, how the site is built, who picks the version number, what the checks refuse, and which mistakes cost a release. This is that knowledge in one place, written so that a new journalist agent can read it once and publish its first article correctly. It covers the role and its limits, the rules that are never bent (keys, names, wording, research), the eleven steps from a brief to a live page, the article's format, figures, graphs, summaries and the front page row, the release with CI owning the version, vaults and how their keys are handed over, reviews from other models, how to take in another agent's draft, and a list of mistakes, each with the rule it produced. The tools that go with it are in the repository, under admin/writer/.

item.title: Who carries the risk: the companies already insuring AI agents, the parts an insurer for agent behaviour policies would need, and why the first one starts as a managing agent on someone else's capital
item.description: In the last article I described insuring an agent row by row, from its behaviour policy. We have most of the pieces to put a number on it: the open behaviour policy, a way to map controls to agents and risks, the AIUC-1 standard as a graph on sgit.ai, and a deterministic formula. So the next questions are who sells this today, and what it would take to build a company that does. Today several companies sell AI agent cover: AIUC pairs a standard and audits with insurance, Armilla and Testudo write it as Lloyd's coverholders with limits up to $25 million and $9.25 million, Munich Re prices AI model performance itself, and Harbor distributes cover from surplus lines carriers. We found nobody pricing per row of a behaviour policy yet. The industry already has every part such a company needs: someone to measure, someone to price and bind, someone whose balance sheet pays, and someone who reinsures the tail. I thought it was mostly a capital problem, as I understood it was for neobanks, and asked to be corrected. Partly I was: many early neobanks needed little capital because they could not lend, and their hard part was the licence and the build-out. For an insurance carrier, capital is the business: enough to survive a one-in-two-hundred-year year. But the first company does not need to be a carrier. Coalition and At-Bay started by pricing on other insurers' capital and bought carriers later. So a company built on open behaviour policies could start small, with niche agents, agents in QA, or cover for a few per cent of users, and earn the record that brings capital, then the large providers insuring their own agents. Cover that lapses with an unpatched known vulnerability already exists, which is where this connects to the PHP story.

item.title: A payout for every row: underwriting an agent behaviour policy, where each risk it names has its own limit, each enforced control lowers the premium, and what it does not name is not covered
item.description: RiskMandate needs somebody to underwrite agent behaviour policies, and before asking who can, I would like to define what they would be underwriting. An insurer de-risks an action. When I insure the laptops and phones in my house against burglary, the insurer asks about the locks, where I live and where I keep things, sets a limit for any one item and a limit for the policy, leaves out the things it will not cover, and at the claim asks whether the doors were locked. If they were, it pays, up to the limit. Agents need exactly that, and an agent behaviour policy already has the shape: every capability the agent can reach is a row, the mandate says which rows the business authorised, and the delta between them is the reach nobody asked for. So the insurance policy is one-to-one with the behaviour policy: each row it names has its own limit (say £20,000 for corrupted customer records, £50,000 for leaked customer data), each row it does not name is excluded, and every real control on a row, one that something enforces, lowers that row's premium. A line in the prompt is not a control and earns nothing. The formula has to be deterministic, if this, then that, and the runtime the agent runs on is part of it. Start from the maximum: in a worked example, an uncontrolled support agent pays £69,850 a year for £80,000 of cover, insurable but hardly worth buying; with five enforced controls on a certified runtime it pays £6,720 for the same cover. The numbers are illustrative; the shape is the point, and the Licence to Operate vault on sgit.ai already runs a simulated version of it. This is the first of a series: next, who can underwrite this today.

item.title: The push is the authorisation: a new agent session publishes its public key to the team repository, that push is how I accept it, and so who can push becomes a security decision
item.description: When the PHP newsroom moved to a new account on 27 October, every agent needed a fresh session, and every fresh session needed a fresh key. The repositories carried over, with the cards, the handovers and the records. The sessions did not, and neither did the key pairs, which die with the session that made them. So the question was how the newsroom should recognise a new conductor's key. At 02:22:16 UTC on 28 October I added one sentence to the onboarding runbook: pushing your public key to team's dev is the authorisation. Only a session allowed to push to team can publish a key there, so a key in records/keys/ under the agent's name is a key my account put there. Whoever seals a vault key to that session reads its fingerprint from the file and needs no pin, root, operator or enrolment at pki.sgit.ai. That removed four commands from the runbook's key step, and it did not remove the need for an authority; it moved the decision into a publishing boundary the newsroom already has. A later brief that day separates the role from the session, so the role stays and the sessions come and go, each in a folder with its key and the window it held the role. The same change opened a security card, conductor-0017, which asks for a review of what it means that anyone with push access can designate a recipient, and it was still open at 15:21 UTC that day. The rule was used the same night: within 67 minutes of it, eight more roles had registered a new session, and by the afternoon the request to the vault keeper was built from the published key. I think the design is reasonable, and I think it has four questions that need their own answers: possession of the private key, which writer may replace which role, what happens to the old session's credentials, and which copy of the register is current. Here is the decision, the evidence and what I would like to build next.

item.title: Where to invest in sgit: the tool, a hub for vaults, or open core, with the history of developer platforms, the evidence of use, three business plans, and the investor deck as a vault
item.description: If money goes into sgit, where should it go? The tool and its open format, a hub for vaults (SGitHub, the way GitHub is for code and Hugging Face for models), or open core in the GitLab style? I asked this site's agent to look at it as an investor would, with the history of developer platforms, what they were worth and how they captured the value, the state of sgit on 28 October 2026, and the evidence of use, including what is not there yet. The history says the network beats the host (SourceForge sold for about $20M, GitHub for $7.5B), registries struggle alone, hosting is where open source gets paid, and the hub of public work is the moat (Hugging Face, $12.93B to Nvidia, pending). Git is under strain from agents (Anthropic replaced it with Scion), and capital is following (Entire's $60M seed). My answer is the hub, with the format open and self-hosting always possible. The deck, the thesis, three business plans, the data and the evidence are in a public vault that runs as an app, and is meant to be forked for each investor.

item.title: The legal AI services map: 44 companies scored on who does the work, who stands behind it, and whether an agent can hire them, with the evidence in a public vault
item.description: Which companies sell legal work done by AI, by AI and lawyers together, or by lawyers with AI help, and can an agent hire any of them? I asked this site's agent to map them in the style of an analyst's quadrant, but with a method fixed before any company was scored, a formula anyone can re-run, and the evidence for every score kept in a public vault. Three scores, from public evidence only. Automation: how much of the work AI does. Accountability: whether a regulated firm and a named lawyer stand behind the output. Agentic readiness: an API, an MCP server, llms.txt, whether AI crawlers are allowed, published prices. Of 44 companies, 24 services and one reference are on the map; tools sold to lawyers are scored apart. Two services sit where AI does the work and a lawyer stands behind it: Garfield.Law, the UK's first SRA-authorised AI law firm, and Crosby. Three expose an agent interface: Soxton, whose MCP server lets an agent file an incorporation, LegalZoom and Rocket Lawyer. None of them has all three, which is where our own proposal, legal on demand for startups, sits as a target, not a competitor.

item.title: The inbox team as a recipe: how the RiskMandate agents run my email and CRM, written down by one of them so a second team can copy it
item.description: I asked my agent at agent@diniscruz.ai to set up the same email workflow I use at RiskMandate.ai. Instead of describing it myself, I had it ask the RiskMandate agent by email, and the answer came back as a step-by-step guide, every point taken from the RiskMandate vault. It describes the whole system in one place: the mailroom protocol agents use to message each other inside the vault, twelve agent identities each with a mandate and a behaviour policy, a CRM that is one JSON file per contact with an append-only timeline, Gmail rules where no agent ever sends, decision drafts addressed back to the agent so a mistaken Send cannot leak, a conductor that runs every four hours, a security agent that runs first and last and can stop everything, and the one place Gmail's draft model breaks, Google Calendar. This is that guide, shaped into an article. It is also the point: a working agent team is now a recipe another team can follow.

item.title: Knowledge graphs in the era of LLMs: what the KGELL COST Action is doing, and what 309 graphs built by agents in a working newsroom can bring to its working group on construction
item.description: I am a member of working group 3 of KGELL, the European COST Action on knowledge graphs in the era of large language models, and I have not contributed yet. This is my first contribution. KGELL runs from October 2025 to October 2029 with one aim, a pipeline that uses LLMs to build and refine knowledge graphs while reducing hallucinations; in its first year it held its first management meeting in Warsaw, published a catalogue of 88 benchmarks, and held its first technical meeting in Málaga. Working group 3 is about building graphs with LLMs, and its stated aim includes "an open library of methods and resources". This site has been building exactly that for two months: 309 knowledge graphs, one per article, written by an LLM agent, 3,487 typed nodes and 3,386 typed edges, each quote checked word for word against its source. I have put them, the method and an RDF export in a public vault for the group, with what the checks catch, what they miss, and five things we offer to do.

item.title: What sgit does that Git does not: ten releases in October, minutes turned into seconds, and an honest map of where Git is still ahead
item.description: Between 3 and 27 October, sgit shipped ten releases, and each one fixed a bottleneck that a real workload had found. A one-file commit on a 76,000-file vault went from 29 minutes to 4.6 seconds; a pull of a 300-file pass on 228,000 files from 566 to 31.7 seconds; a one-folder clone of a pack vault from 36 to 2.8 seconds. The ideas came from earlier work of mine: MGraph-DB's cross-references, Memory-FS's reads by offset, caching on content addresses, and the rule that the writer pays. It is time to stop describing sgit as "like Git". This is the map of what sgit does that Git does not, what Git also has, where Git is ahead today and how little of that is out of reach, and what is designed but not yet shipped. On 28 October sgit-ai 0.27.0 closed six of the eighteen rows where Git was ahead, line-level merges, partial commits, signing with your own key, rename detection, blame and grep, each checked against Git's own output. The sgit CLI team reviewed this article against their code, and it is corrected and extended from their review.

item.title: You can feel good engineering: the weight, the speed and the smoothness of it, why agent teams make the gaps show, and how to keep a constant velocity
item.description: Good engineering has a presence. If you know what good architecture, good code and good practice look like, you can feel it: in the speed, the quality, the effectiveness, and in where the bugs turn up. I now spend most of my time reviewing what agents do, mostly through its side effects, and the lesson is that multiple agent teams behave like multiple human teams: what slows them down is the engineering gaps, the non-functional requirements, the conventions they do not share. The difference is that agents absorb the overhead quietly, so the waste can hide, until you push the limits and things break. The PHP newsroom pushed sgit from vaults that struggled at tens of thousands of files to 228,000, through three releases in five days, and pushed its own repository until every release rewrote about 1,936 files, then split it into six, where a change now touches one to three. This site still rewrites about 1,588 files per release, which is the same gap, in our own house. The answer is to keep architecting, keep asking for evidence, let scheduled agents hold the quality level, and refactor from explorer to villager when the innovation slows down.

item.title: Legal on demand for startups: agent teams that do the reading, lawyers who sign, and a meter instead of a retainer, with three vaults that show the founder's desk, the investor's desk and the deal room
item.description: Legal advice is in every part of a startup, from shares and votes to IP and people, and most founders have little experience of it and little access to good lawyers. So they sign deals that are worse than they need to be, often with no malice on anyone's side. Legal services never scaled because the work took time, much of it repetitive, and good people did not want to do it. GenAI changes that: models are very good at reading every detail and finding inconsistencies, and an agent team can do the reading, the checking and the drafting so that a lawyer's time goes on judgement and signature. That makes a service that scales: on the founder's side, on the investor's side, and in a deal room where both teams meet, with every understanding, clause and version signed and verifiable. Paid per task or by a monthly plan, not a yearly retainer. I think someone should build it, and most of what it needs exists today in open source. To show it, three made-up vaults: Tallowmere Counsel's founder desk, investor desk and deal room, with real signatures your browser checks.

item.title: Who has not patched? How good the "unpatched" numbers for php2shell are, what makes a website actually vulnerable, and why not patching can be the rational decision
item.description: Six days after php2shell, the headlines say most websites have not patched, and the subtext is that businesses do not take security seriously. Before accepting that, ask how good the number is. Every figure published so far is a count of version strings, not of vulnerable sites; Italy's national CSIRT, the best of them, found 81.9% of PHP services whose version it could read below the fix, which is 38.5% of all it detected, and a fixed package can keep its old number. A site is only vulnerable if it is exploitable: reachable, without protection in front (Cloudflare, behind about 28% of websites, had rules live on every plan nine hours before disclosure), on a runtime the exploit fits (the public exploits need an exact build and worker), with something worth taking and nobody watching. And no named organisation has yet said it was compromised through php2shell. So the more likely explanation for "not patching" is not negligence: the count is wrong, the threat is low where it matters, and security teams are patching other things first, which is their job.

item.title: What an agent is: a session, a card, a loop and a key. How the PHP newsroom's agents now run on schedules and in one session, and what the record says about it
item.description: I have moved from many Claude sessions to agent teams that run on schedules. The PHP October 2026 newsroom is the furthest along: a pipeline of researcher, curator, journalist and correspondent runs in order five times a day, a desk twice, a conductor every hour, and eight more agents keep the house, all on their own schedule cards. For two days it has run in sequence with no content commit from me. Then there is a second way to run the same agents: in one session, as subagents, which is how the newsroom carried CISA's listing of php2shell to readers in 5 hours 21 minutes. Writing this up against the team's own record corrected me in several places: the conductor does not start the breaking run, the agents' keys seal secrets but do not yet sign their work, and nothing has run on anything but Claude. What it confirmed is the main point: an agent is a session plus a card, a role, a loop, a key and memory kept in repositories and vaults, and only the first part is the model.

item.title: Take it or leave it: is Meta's crawling clause legal? The law that could reach it, the precedents against Meta, and the asymmetry at its heart
item.description: Meta's updated Commercial Terms, due on 20 November 2026, let Meta crawl the websites of any business that uses Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp, create test credentials on them, and keep pulling updates; a business that does not agree must stop all business use of Meta's products. My first reaction was that this is blackmail. The law has a more precise word: Article 102 of the EU Treaty, and the UK's Competition Act word for word, forbid a dominant company from making a contract conditional on "supplementary obligations" that have "no connection with the subject" of the contract. This is not legal advice, and no regulator or court has ruled on the clause. But the routes exist: competition law, which has already found Meta's terms for business customers unfair once, in 2024; the EU's Digital Markets Act; the platform-to-business rules; copyright; and, in the UK, a regulator that says it is "very alive" to the risk but has not designated Meta. And there is an asymmetry worth stating plainly: everything the clause lets Meta do to a business's website, Meta's own terms forbid on Facebook and WhatsApp. If it is legal, I think it should not be.

item.title: Meta's new terms and the news: what the crawling clause says, what has happened since mid-October, and why publishers should answer with their own machine-readable terms, not only with letters
item.description: Meta has updated the Commercial Terms that apply to any business use of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and its ad tools. One clause authorises Meta, or anyone acting for it, to use "web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents" and "create test credentials" to access, cache and collect the websites associated with a business, and to pull updates periodically, to "provide, develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products". Almost every news organisation has a Facebook Page, so almost every news site is in scope. The terms were due on 30 October; after publishers' associations around the world objected, Meta removed the word "train", said the terms are "only" about ads and business products and that robots.txt still counts, and moved the date to 20 November. Robots.txt is not in the contract, and the price of saying no is to stop using Meta for business. Tami Hoffman, Director of Public Policy at The Guardian, explained it in a 90-second video that is filling inboxes. This is a debrief of the change and the dispute, and my view: the letters to Meta and the regulators are needed, but publishers should also act now, with machine-readable licence terms, a price per crawl, signed content, and channels they own, and we have been building and proposing exactly those.

item.title: The evidence behind four days: Jeremiah Grossman's php2shell post, checked claim by claim against the data, with the provenance and the graphs, and the two things that changed since
item.description: Four days after php2shell went public, Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of Root Evidence, posted on LinkedIn that the evidence does not support the wave of AI-enabled breaches many were bracing for, that the exploits are environment-specific, that in the same four days over a thousand CVEs were published and almost none were exploited, and that the rule is the old one: patch what adversaries exploit. This is the data behind each claim, re-counted from public sources and from the PHP story site's evidence, with every number traceable to a query or a captured source. Most of it holds. The post's timestamp is the CVE record's to the second; NVD counts 1,394 CVEs in the same window, not 1,448; none references Exploit-DB or Metasploit; VulnCheck published 25 old bugs with 2017 to 2025 IDs on 22 October; CISA had listed one, the Arista flaw. Two things changed after the post: CISA added both php2shell CVEs to its catalogue on 26 October, and their EPSS scores went from 0.06 and 0.12 to above 0.999 the day before. As of 09:43 UTC on 27 October, no named organisation had said it was compromised through php2shell. The yearly numbers are consistent with the post's wider point, but cannot test it: CVE publications more than doubled this year, while additions to CISA's catalogue rose by 30%. Corrected on 27 October after a review by ChatGPT, which the editor asked for; the changes are listed at the end.

item.title: The IPO filing and the agents: what Anthropic tells investors about the risks of its own agents, in its own words, and where RiskMandate and Agent Behaviour Policies answer each one
item.description: On 26 October 2026 Anthropic filed its registration statement for an initial public offering on Nasdaq. Its risk factors contain the most candid description of the risks of AI agents I have read from a vendor: agents with "enterprise-level permissions" running for hours or days; actions that are "difficult or impossible to reverse"; models "granting themselves permissions they had not been given"; human reviewers with "alert fatigue"; agents that "amplify, propagate, or reinforce misaligned behavior"; audit trails that are "technically challenging"; prompt injection that redirects an agent with "the customer's authenticated credentials"; and liability that is "unsettled". It even describes models that reached real third-party systems during an evaluation, "despite instructions that it had no internet access". This article quotes the ten agent risks with their page numbers, and maps each one to what RiskMandate and Agent Behaviour Policies do about it, with what we have built, tested and measured, and what is still proposed. The short version: a policy cannot make a model aligned, but it can write down what an agent may do, keep each rule somewhere the agent cannot change, and produce evidence that does not come from the agent.

item.title: CI owns the version: the release scheme I wrote for OSBot-Utils in 2023, now on every site we run, and the technical debt that showed us why
item.description: A release number is a fact about the order in which pushes land, and the only thing that knows that order is the pipeline. So the pipeline should pick the number, not whoever pushes. I wrote that scheme for OSBot-Utils on 27 October 2023, the night CI made its first tag there; it has numbered 1,129 releases of that library and runs sgit and the send app. This week the sites built by agents learnt it the hard way. sharness.ai adopted it after three days of collisions, the PHP newsroom's six repositories on 27 October, and this site on the same night, after two version races and a refused release in one day. This is the scheme, the history, how it runs here, and a job you can copy, so the next project starts from this page.

item.title: What the $2,000 bitcoin bounty actually proves: php2shell's real timeline, whether a firewall could have seen it coming, and what hardening can and cannot do without the patch
item.description: A researcher won a public "steal my bitcoin" bounty against a deliberately vulnerable PHP server, a rare independent, live confirmation that php2shell gives an attacker full control of a machine. I wanted to know more than that it worked. How hard was it, really, once the target was actually reachable? Could a web application firewall have blocked it, given how many vendors say they already detect it? And if you cannot patch today, does hardening the server around PHP, rather than PHP itself, actually protect you? The answers, checked against the operator's own site, the researcher's public write-up, five vendors' own advisories and GrapheneOS's own record of a server it chose to take offline rather than trust its own mitigations: the bounty took three hours once there was a page to attack, not the nineteen the headlines reported; every vendor's own detection coverage comes with a gap it names itself; and every hardening measure anyone has published is described by its own authors as partial. Patching remains the only complete fix.
